item.title: 10. Matrix Taxonomy: Definitions and Identities
item.description:
Matrices are classified by shape, symmetry, and special algebraic properties; these determine eigenvalue structure and which factorizations apply.

Elementary structural forms

  • Identity $I$: $a_{ij} = 1$ if $i=j$, else $0$. $AI = IA = A$.
  • Diagonal $D$: $a_{ij} = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Eigenvalues = diagonal entries; $\det(D) = \prod_i d_{ii}$.
  • Scalar matrix: $A = cI$ (all diagonal entries equal).
  • Triangular: Upper $U$: $a_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$. Lower $L$: $a_{ij}=0$ for $i<j$. For any triangular matrix, $\det = \prod_i a_{ii}$.

Symmetry-based matrices

  • Symmetric ($A = A^T$): Real eigenvalues; orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues; always diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$.
  • Skew-symmetric ($A = -A^T$): Diagonal entries $0$; eigenvalues purely imaginary or zero; if $n$ is odd, $\det(A)=0$.
  • Hermitian ($A = A^H = \overline{A}^T$): Complex analogue of symmetric; $\mathbf{x}^H A \mathbf{x}$ is real for all $\mathbf{x}$.

Transformation-based matrices

  • Orthogonal $Q$: $Q^T Q = Q Q^T = I$, so $Q^{-1} = Q^T$. Columns/rows are orthonormal; preserves dot products and norms ($|Q\mathbf{x}| = |\mathbf{x}|$); $\det(Q) = \pm 1$.
  • Unitary $U$: $U^H U = I$ (complex analogue of orthogonal).
  • Permutation $P$: Obtained by reordering rows of $I$; $P^T = P^{-1}$; $\det(P) = \pm 1$ (sign of permutation).

Operational properties

  • Idempotent: $A^2 = A$ (e.g., projection matrices); eigenvalues in ${0,1}$.
  • Nilpotent: $A^k = \mathbf{0}$ for some $k$; all eigenvalues $0$; $\text{tr}(A)=\det(A)=0$.
  • Involutory: $A^2 = I$ (e.g., reflections); eigenvalues in ${1,-1}$.
  • Normal: $A A^H = A^H A$; includes symmetric, skew-symmetric, orthogonal, unitary; normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable.

Singularity and definiteness

  • Singular: $\det(A)=0$; not invertible; at least one eigenvalue $0$.
  • Non-singular: $\det(A) \neq 0$; full rank; invertible.
  • Defective: Fewer than $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors; not diagonalizable.
  • Positive definite ($A \succ 0$): $\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$; all eigenvalues $> 0$.
  • Positive semi-definite ($A \succeq 0$): $\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} \ge 0$; all eigenvalues $\ge 0$.

Positive definiteness appears in covariance matrices, Hessians at minima, and stability of linear systems.
